Dermatology · published research

Corticosteroid addiction dermatitis

A 170-person retrospective series reported symptom relief after red-light treatment during topical steroid withdrawal, but the combined care and lack of a control group prevent attribution to light alone.

PBM Database summary

What the records report

A 170-person retrospective series reported symptom relief after red-light treatment during topical steroid withdrawal, but the combined care and lack of a control group prevent attribution to light alone.

Summary of the Evidence

One publication reports an uncontrolled retrospective series of 170 Asian patients with facial corticosteroid addiction dermatitis. Two participants also had pre- and post-treatment biopsies, but those observations belong to the same cohort. No controlled replication was identified.

Human and clinical evidence

Participants stopped topical corticosteroids, received red-light treatment, and were advised to use liquid emollient. At two weeks after treatment, 85.9% reported some relief, including smaller lesion area or improved symptoms. Response was reported as greater in acute than chronic lesions and among people receiving more sessions. Of 137 patients with follow-up, 107 reported no topical steroid or other medication use for three to six months. No adverse events were observed in this series (Luan et al. 2014).

Animal evidence

No animal study was identified.

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

No standalone cell or ex-vivo study was identified. Biopsies from two participants showed epidermal healing and reduced dermal inflammation. They are descriptive findings within the uncontrolled cohort, not independent evidence.

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The clinic used a 633-nm LED, red visible light, for 20 minutes every other day. Steroid withdrawal and emollient use accompanied treatment, and there was no comparator. The study cannot identify which part of care produced the changes or whether the schedule transfers to other settings.

Interpretation

The series describes improvement during combined withdrawal and light care but cannot show that PBM caused it. A controlled comparison using the same withdrawal and skin-care plan with or without active light is needed.

Evidence strength in source summaryVery low for symptom improvement after topical steroid withdrawal
Publications and records1 article

Evidence strength rationale and next steps

The 170-person series is relatively large for this topic, but it had no comparison group and light was started alongside steroid withdrawal and emollient care. The response rate cannot isolate the effect of light from these changes or the condition’s course. A controlled study with a standardized withdrawal plan, independent outcome assessment, and longer follow-up would support a stronger rating.
